fetched_contents.text: Non-pharmacological therapy for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neurotoxicity: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials Abstract Background Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neurotoxicity (CIPN) is the most common adverse effect in patients undergoing chemotherapy, and no effective interventions are currently available for its prevention and treatment. Non-pharmacological therapies appear to be beneficial for the prevention and treatment of CIPN, but it remains unclear which therapy is most effective. The aim of this study was to identify the most effective non-pharmacological therapy for CIPN patients. Methods PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched for randomized controlled trials on non-pharmacological therapies for CIPN. The primary outcomes included pain and peripheral neuropathological symptoms, and the secondary outcomes included quality of life, sensory and motor symptoms. The pairwise analysis and a network meta-analysis were performed using a random effects model. Results A total of 46 articles were included in this study, involving 2,878 participants. Our study showed that massage was more effective in pain-alleviating compared with acupuncture [SMD = 0.81, 95%CI (0.04, 1.57)], vitamin and gabapentin [SMD = 2.56, 95%CI (1.39, 3.74)], and usual care and placebo [SMD = 0.9, 95%CI (0.31, 1.49)]. As for attenuating peripheral neuropathological symptoms, massage was more effective than usual care and placebo [SMD = 0.75, 95%CI (0.33, 1.17)], sensorimotor training [SMD = 1.17, 95%CI (0.24, 2.10)], electrostimulation [SMD=-1.18, 95%CI (-2.14, -0.21)], multimodal exercise [SMD=-0.82, 95%CI (-1.57, -0.08)], and resistance training [SMD = 1.03, 95%CI (0.11, 1.95)]. Massage was also more effective than other non-pharmacological therapies in improving quality of life, sensory and motor symptoms. Conclusions According to our study, massage has advantages in alleviating pain, improving quality of life, and improving peripheral neuropathological symptoms and has better effect than other non-pharmacological interventions, representing certain clinical significance. However, the results of this study should be interpreted with caution due to the limitations of the included studies. In the future, more high-quality multi arm randomized controlled trials can be attempted to provide direct comparisons of the relative effects of non-pharmacological interventions. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12883-023-03485-z. Keywords: Chemotherapy, Adjuvant, Peripheral nervous system diseases, Randomized controlled trial Introduction Chemotherapy is one of the most commonly used anti-cancer treatments. Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) refers to a dose-limiting adverse effect that commonly occurs in patients receiving neurotoxic chemotherapies such as taxane, platinum agents, vinca alkaloids, thalidomide, and bortezomib. CIPN is clinically characterized by varying degrees of sensory, motor, and autonomic nervous dysfunction. Sensory symptoms occur firstly in the extremities as numbness, pain, or burning sensation, with a “sock-and-glove-like” distribution. Loss of vibration sense and joint position sense could be observed in severe cases, and it affects gait and balance, thereby exerting an adverse impact on patients’ quality of life [1]. The incidence of motor symptoms is lower than that of sensory symptoms. Motor symptoms typically included distal limb weakness, gait and balance dysfunction. Autonomic nervous dysfunction is characterized by orthostatic hypotension, constipation, sexual dysfunction, etc. A review on CIPN has proposed that CIPN could occur in approximately 30-40% of patients receiving neurotoxic chemotherapy [2], and the effects of CIPN on the nervous system depend on the types of chemotherapeutic agents, pharmacological properties, and accumulated dose. A study has shown that 30% of CIPN patients could not recover from chemotherapy six months after chemotherapy [3]. The 2020 updated clinical practice guideline released by the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) indicates that there is currently no pharmacological agent capable of preventing CIPN, and evidence of moderate quality recommends duloxetine for patients with CIPN-associated pain after chemotherapy [4]. To date, the treatment of CIPN is still under exploration. Recent evidence has revealed that non-pharmacological therapies, such as exercise, acupuncture, pressure therapy, and scrambler therapy seem to be of potential benefits [4]. Previous studies have reported that acupuncture, massage, and pedilavium could alleviate the symptoms of CIPN [5]. Moreover, a meta-analysis on acupuncture indicates that acupuncture could effectively attenuate the pain and dysfunction in CIPN patients [6]. Another study has assessed the effect of exercise on peripheral neuropathological symptoms and reported that sensorimotor training could improve static balance, quality of life, and neuropathological symptoms in CIPN patients [7]. However, these studies focus on a single certain therapy for CIPN, lacking a systematical comparison among various non-pharmacological therapies. The current study is the first network meta-analysis (NMA) to assess the comparative effects of non-pharmacological therapies for the treatment of CIPN. Through the NMA approach, we can summarize the direct and indirect evidence and perform pairwise comparisons between different interventions. This study has included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluate the efficacy of non-pharmacological interventions for CIPN patients, with other conventional treatments like placebo, or other non-pharmacological interventions as controls and pain, neuropathological symptoms, quality of life, sensory and motor symptoms as outcome measures. fetched_contents.text: An update on non-pharmacological interventions for pain relief Summary Chronic pain affects a substantial portion of the population, yet current treatments often fail to provide adequate relief. Non-pharmacological interventions, which target behaviors and brain processes underlying the experience of pain, hold promises in offering relief for people with chronic pain. This review consolidates the current knowledge concerning the efficacy of non-pharmacological interventions for chronic pain. We focus on psychological interventions (e.g., cognitive behavioral therapy-based interventions and emotion-based therapies) that use mental techniques and physical practices (e.g., exercise, massage, acupuncture, and yoga) that use body techniques to reduce pain. The efficacy of neuromodulation is also discussed. Given that placebo and expectation effects may enhance benefits for non-pharmacological interventions, we also discuss placebo interventions and expectation management practices. Finally, we describe digital therapeutics as an emerging approach for managing chronic pain. We argue that non-pharmacological interventions are critical adjunctive or stand-alone interventions for chronic pain conditions. Keywords: cognitive behavioral therapy, exercise, neuromodulation, placebo effects, expectations, extended reality and therapeutic digital applications Graphical abstract ---------------------------------------- Non-pharmacological interventions, such as psychological approaches, physical therapy, neuromodulation, placebo-induced hypoalgesia, expectation management, and XR therapeutics, offer potential for managing chronic pain. However, the long-term benefits of these interventions remain dependent on necessary lifestyle changes, and further research is needed to explore the combined effects of these interventions. Introduction Chronic pain presents a pervasive challenge worldwide, incurring significant individual and societal burdens. Estimates of its prevalence in the population range from approximately 20% to 40%.1,2 Chronic pain, irrespective of its etiology, detrimentally affects quality of life and imposes substantial economic costs, with estimates in the United States alone ranging from $560 to $635 billion annually in 2010 constant dollars. About one in fourteen adults are experiencing high-impact chronic pain,3 which is defined as having pain most days during the past 3 months together with limitations in daily life or work activities because of pain.4 While medications represent the most common treatment approach for chronic pain, with various pharmaceutical classes recommended as first-, second-, or third-line options for chronic neuropathic pain management,5 non-pharmacological interventions are often relegated to the status of last resort or are mentioned as considerations. However, many chronic pain patients do not achieve clinically significant pain relief through medication alone. A recent meta-analysis evaluating the efficacy of opioids for chronic pain found only marginal improvements in pain intensity compared to placebo.6 Similarly, a systematic review on drug efficacy for neuropathic pain management suggested that the efficacy estimates of antidepressants and antiepileptics seem to have decreased with more recent large sample size randomized controlled trials (RCTs).7 Our narrative review will discuss an array of non-pharmacological approaches for managing chronic pain in adults, highlighting interventions with evidence for efficacy or effectiveness, patient acceptability, and potential mechanisms (Figure 1). These approaches will be considered independently of the pain type—whether neuropathic, nociplastic, or nociceptive (for definitions, see Box 1). Recognizing that diverse mechanisms underlie these interventions, we will address the challenge of unifying them under a single conceptual framework by adapting and expanding the embodied view of pain framework.8 Box 1. Chronic pain generally affects quality of life and functionality. * (2) Neuropathic pain: pain caused by a lesion of disease of the somatosensory system. Neuropathic pain is often severe and disabling. * (3) Nociceptive pain: this type of pain is caused by tissue damage or inflammation. It is usually well localized and can be either somatic (affecting the skin, muscles, bones, or joints) or visceral (affecting internal organs). This narrative review summarises the current literature on the efficacy and safety of physiotherapy to reduce pain and disability in people with radicular pain and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, 2 common peripheral neuropathies. For chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, the current evidence based on 8 randomised controlled trials suggests that exercise may reduce symptoms in patients with established neuropathy, but there is a lack of evidence for its preventative effect in patients who do not yet have symptoms. For radicular pain, most of the 21 trials investigated interventions targeted at improving motor control or reducing neural mechanosensitivity. The results were equivocal, with some indication that neural tissue management may show some benefits in reducing pain. Adverse events to physiotherapy seemed rare; however, these were not consistently reported across all studies. Although it is encouraging to see that the evidence base for physiotherapy in the treatment of peripheral neuropathic pain is growing steadily, the mixed quality of available studies currently prevents firm treatment recommendations. Based on promising preliminary data, suggestions are made on potential directions to move the field forward. 1. Common systemic neuropathies include chemotherapy-induced neuropathy and diabetic neuropathy. The most prevalent focal neuropathies include entrapment neuropathies such as carpal tunnel syndrome, radiculopathy, and radicular pain. To date, treatment for patients with peripheral neuropathies and neuropathic pain has relied largely on pharmacology. However, recent reviews suggest that the efficacy of neuropathic pain medications is only modest and often accompanied by adverse drug responses.23,39 Physiotherapy management for patients with peripheral neuropathies has gained increasing interest in the past decade, but evidence for its efficacy and safety is only starting to emerge.21,42,74 The aim of this narrative review is to describe the current evidence for the efficacy and safety of physiotherapy to reduce pain and disability in patients with peripheral neuropathies and to suggest future directions for research. fetched_contents.text: Multimodal non-invasive non-pharmacological therapies for chronic pain: mechanisms and progress Abstract Background Chronic pain conditions impose significant burdens worldwide. Pharmacological treatments like opioids have limitations. Non-invasive non-pharmacological therapies (NINPT) encompass diverse interventions including physical, psychological, complementary and alternative approaches, and other innovative techniques that provide analgesic options for chronic pain without medications. Main body This review elucidates the mechanisms of major NINPT modalities and synthesizes evidence for their clinical potential across chronic pain populations. NINPT leverages peripheral, spinal, and supraspinal mechanisms to restore normal pain processing and limit central sensitization. However, heterogeneity in treatment protocols and individual responses warrants optimization through precision medicine approaches. Conclusion Future adoption of NINPT requires addressing limitations in standardization and accessibility as well as synergistic combination with emerging therapies. Overall, this review highlights the promise of NINPT as a valuable complementary option ready for integration into contemporary pain medicine paradigms to improve patient care and outcomes. Keywords: Pain, Non-invasive non-pharmacological therapies, Physical modalities, Psychological interventions, Complementary and alternative therapies, TENS, CBT, TMS, VR Background Chronic pain conditions, such as osteoarthritis, diabetic neuropathy, and fibromyalgia, refer to a range of complex and multifaceted disorders that affect millions of individuals worldwide and impose significant burdens on society, healthcare systems, and personal well-being [1, 2]. The management of chronic pain presents a major challenge for healthcare professionals and researchers, as there is no single or universally effective treatment and patients often suffer from chronic pain for a long period of time [3, 4]. Furthermore, conventional treatments such as opioids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) carry significant risks and limitations, including addiction, tolerance, dependence, gastrointestinal bleeding, renal impairment, and cardiovascular events, especially when used long term [5, 6]. As a result, additional approaches are needed to provide safe and effective chronic pain relief without causing harm or adverse effects [7]. Non-invasive non-pharmacological therapies (NINPT) offer options for managing chronic pain safely and effectively without damaging tissues or causing significant side effects [8]. For chronic pain conditions, NINPT can be categorized into physical modalities, psychological interventions, complementary and alternative therapies, and other innovative techniques [8, 9]. Physical modalities like transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), heat therapy and cryotherapy, and massage aim to modulate chronic pain signals through physiological mechanisms [10–12]. Psychological interventions including cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and mindfulness-based therapy help patients cope with chronic pain by promoting positive psychological and behavioral changes [13–15]. Complementary and alternative therapies such as acupuncture, yoga, and music therapy provide additional approaches to reducing chronic pain through mechanisms involving both physical and psychological aspects [16–18]. Other interventions like chiropractic care, biofeedback, and virtual reality (VR) therapy employ techniques to modulate chronic pain [19–21]. For chronic pain management, NINPT can be used alone or combined with conventional treatments based on specific conditions, patient preferences, and availability of resources. Furthermore, understanding the mechanisms underlying how NINPT alleviate chronic pain is critical for optimizing their clinical application. To begin with, it helps establish the causal relationship between NINPT and their effects on chronic pain, clarifying their validity and reliability [15, 22]. Secondly, elucidating the mechanisms of NINPT action allows for optimized, individualized therapeutic regimens meeting the needs of each patient. This includes determining the optimal frequency, intensity, and duration for achieving the best outcomes [23]. Thirdly, it spurs continued innovation in developing more effective and integrative NINPT modalities for chronic pain relief through emerging technologies [7, 24]. Lastly, establishing the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying the effects of NINPT on chronic pain enables the development of evidence-based clinical guidelines on recommending appropriate NINPT options for different chronic pain conditions [9, 25]. The objective of this review is to provide a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of various NINPT for chronic pain management, with a focus on their mechanisms of action and clinical applications. For each modality, we discuss how they modulate pain signaling across peripheral, spinal, and supraspinal levels. We also highlight limitations, challenges, and future directions for optimizing the use of NINPT. We aim to build a bridge between basic research on mechanisms of NINPT and their clinical implementation for chronic pain relief. Elucidating the neurophysiological processes underlying this maladaptive transition across molecular, cellular, and systems levels will inform targeted interventions. ## Which non-pharmacological approaches have the strongest evidence for managing platinum-induced neuropathic pain?

The evidence base for non-pharmacological management of platinum-induced neuropathic pain is strongest for massage, multimodal exercise, and multimodal non-invasive non-pharmacological therapies (NINPT), while acupuncture, heat therapy, and TENS show some support but with less consistent or weaker evidence.

### 1) Massage: strongest direct evidence
The network meta-analysis on chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) found that **massage had the largest effect size among non-pharmacological interventions** in the included studies. It was more effective than acupuncture, vitamin plus gabapentin, usual care, and placebo for **pain alleviation** [SMD = 0.81, 95%CI (0.04, 1.57)] [N1-F1]. It was also more effective than usual care and placebo for **peripheral neuropathological symptoms** [SMD = 0.75, 95%CI (0.33, 1.17)] and more effective than sensorimotor training, electrostimulation, multimodal exercise, resistance training, and other non-pharmacological therapies for improving quality of life, sensory and motor symptoms [N1-F1]. This makes massage the intervention with the most directly supported evidence in the provided literature.

### 2) Multimodal exercise and multimodal non-pharmacological approaches
The same network meta-analysis found that **multimodal exercise** was less effective than massage, with a negative SMD of −0.82, 95%CI (−1.57, −0.08) for peripheral neuropathological symptoms [N1-F1]. However, the evidence for multimodal non-invasive non-pharmacological therapies is broader. The review on NINPT states that these therapies can be used alone or in combination and that they include physical, psychological, complementary, and alternative approaches, such as TENS, heat therapy, cryotherapy, massage, CBT, mindfulness, acupuncture, yoga, and other innovative techniques [N6-F4]. It also notes that recent clinical trials demonstrate **heat therapy reduces neuropathic pain in chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy** [N6-R2], which is directly relevant to platinum-induced neuropathy.

### 3) TENS and heat therapy
Heat therapy is specifically highlighted in the chronic pain review as having **recent clinical trial evidence** for reducing neuropathic pain in conditions like diabetic neuropathy and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy [N6-R2]. TENS is also part of the broader NINPT category, where physical modalities aim to modulate chronic pain signals through physiological mechanisms [N6-F4]. However, the provided evidence does not give a direct effect size for TENS in platinum-induced neuropathy, so its support is indirect rather than as strong as massage.

### 4) Acupuncture and other complementary therapies
Acupuncture is supported by the chronic pain review as part of the complementary and alternative therapy category, which provides additional approaches to reducing chronic pain through physical and psychological mechanisms [N2-F2]. The review also notes that acupuncture is one of the non-pharmacological methods used for millennia to relieve pain [N2-R2]. However, the evidence provided here is more general than specific to platinum-induced neuropathy. In the CIPN network meta-analysis, acupuncture was among the interventions compared with massage and was not shown to be more effective than massage for pain or peripheral neuropathological symptoms [N1-F1]. So, acupuncture is promising but not the strongest-supported intervention in the current evidence base.

### 5) Spinal cord stimulation
Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is discussed in the context of neuropathic pain, but the evidence provided is limited. The chronic pain review notes that SCS can be used for neuropathic pain and that some studies suggest it may be effective for peripheral neuropathic pain [N6-F4]. The spinal cord stimulation search excerpt also notes that patients with neuropathic pain responded better to stimulation than those with nociceptive pain, but it does not provide a direct comparison with platinum-induced neuropathy [N7-R1]. Therefore, SCS appears plausible for neuropathic pain, but the evidence here is insufficient to rank it as one of the strongest supported non-pharmacological approaches.

### 6) Combined multimodal approaches
The NINPT review emphasizes that NINPT can be used alone or combined with conventional treatments, and that multimodal approaches are being increasingly explored [N6-F4]. The same review also highlights that multimodal approaches may have greater clinical potential than single interventions because they can target pain at multiple levels—peripheral, spinal, and supraspinal [N6-F4]. However, the provided evidence does not present a direct comparative trial of a multimodal package specifically for platinum-induced neuropathy, so this remains an important but indirect conclusion.

### 7) Outcomes and clinical meaning
The most important outcomes measured in the strongest evidence are **pain**, **peripheral neuropathological symptoms**, **quality of life**, and **sensory and motor symptoms** [N1-F1]. These outcomes matter clinically because they capture both symptom relief and functional improvement. The fact that massage was more effective than usual care and placebo for pain and neuropathological symptoms suggests it may be more useful in everyday clinical practice than interventions with only mixed or weaker support [N1-F1].

### Bottom line
If you must rank the interventions by evidence strength in the provided sources, the order is:
1. **Massage** — strongest direct evidence from a network meta-analysis [N1-F1]
2. **Multimodal exercise** — weaker than massage, but still part of the multimodal evidence base [N1-F1]
3. **Heat therapy** — recent clinical trial evidence for neuropathic pain in CIPN [N6-R2]
4. **TENS** — part of NINPT but with less direct evidence in the provided sources [N6-F4]
5. **Acupuncture** — promising but not as strongly supported in the current evidence [N2-F2, N1-F1]
6. **Spinal cord stimulation** — plausible for neuropathic pain, but limited evidence in the provided sources [N6-F4, N7-R1]

Overall, the evidence suggests that massage and multimodal approaches are the most promising, but the quality and consistency of support vary across interventions [N1-F1, N6-F4].

## Biological and physiological rationale for each promising non-pharmacological approach

The evidence points to several mechanisms by which non-pharmacological approaches may reduce pain and improve function in neuropathies. These mechanisms overlap in important ways with the pathophysiology of platinum-induced neuropathy, but mechanistic understanding remains incomplete in many cases.

### 1) Massage: peripheral and central modulation
The chronic pain review states that physical modalities like massage aim to modulate chronic pain signals through physiological mechanisms [N6-F4]. In the CIPN network meta-analysis, massage was more effective than usual care and placebo for pain and peripheral neuropathological symptoms [N1-F1]. Biologically, massage may reduce pain through:
- **Mechanical stimulation** of soft tissues, which can reduce local inflammation and improve blood flow [N6-F4].
- **Gate-control theory** effects, where tactile input may inhibit pain signals before they reach the central nervous system [N6-F4].
- **Anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects**, which may be especially relevant for CIPN, where chemotherapeutic agents can damage peripheral nerves and cause neuropathic pain [N1-F1].

This aligns with the platinum-induced neuropathy pathology, which involves peripheral nerve injury and dysfunction, as well as altered sensory and motor signaling [N1-F1].

### 2) Physical therapy/exercise: sensorimotor control and neuroplasticity
The physiotherapy review for painful peripheral neuropathies states that physiotherapy and exercise may reduce pain and disability in patients with CIPN and other neuropathies [N3-F3]. It notes that exercise may reduce symptoms in established CIPN, though there is limited evidence for prevention [N3-F3]. The review also emphasizes that interventions targeted at improving motor control or reducing neural mechanosensitivity were common in studies of radicular pain [N3-F3].

Biologically, exercise may help through:
- **Neuroplasticity**: repeated movement training may strengthen neural circuits and improve sensorimotor function [N3-F3].
- **Muscle activation and proprioception**: strengthening and motor-control exercises can improve balance and stability, which is especially important in neuropathic patients [N3-F3].
- **Improved circulation**: exercise can enhance blood flow and reduce ischemia-related pain [N6-F4].

These mechanisms overlap with platinum-induced neuropathy, where motor and sensory dysfunction, balance impairment, and reduced quality of life are common [N1-F1].

### 3) Heat therapy: peripheral analgesia and inflammatory modulation
The chronic pain review explicitly notes that heat therapy is part of physical modalities that modulate chronic pain signals through physiological mechanisms [N6-F4]. It also states that recent clinical trials demonstrate heat therapy reduces neuropathic pain in conditions like diabetic neuropathy and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy [N6-R2].

Biologically, heat therapy may work by:
- **Increasing local blood flow** and reducing tissue ischemia [N6-F4].
- **Modulating pain signaling** at the peripheral level, possibly through temperature-sensitive ion channels and neuroinflammation [N6-F4].
- **Reducing inflammatory mediators** that contribute to neuropathic pain [N6-F4].

This is especially relevant to platinum-induced neuropathy, which is often associated with microvascular and inflammatory changes in peripheral nerves [N1-F1].

### 4) Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)
TENS is part of the broader NINPT category and is described as a physical modality that modulates chronic pain signals through physiological mechanisms [N6-F4]. The chronic pain review also notes that neuromodulation is discussed as part of non-pharmacological interventions [N2-F2].

Biologically, TENS may work by:
- **Gate-control effects**: electrical stimulation may inhibit pain transmission at the spinal level [N6-F4].
- **Endogenous opioid release**: stimulation may activate descending inhibitory pathways [N6-F4].
- **Modulation of peripheral and central sensitization** [N6-F4].

However, the provided evidence does not give a direct effect size for TENS in platinum-induced neuropathy, so its mechanism is well-supported in theory but less directly established for this specific condition [N6-F4].

### 5) Acupuncture
Acupuncture is described in the chronic pain review as part of complementary and alternative therapies that provide additional approaches to reducing chronic pain through mechanisms involving both physical and psychological aspects [N2-F2]. It is also noted as a method used for millennia to relieve pain [N2-R2].

Biologically, acupuncture may work through:
- **Gate-control and endogenous analgesia** pathways [N2-F2].
- **Neurotransmitter release**, including opioids and endorphins [N2-F2].
- **Anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects** [N2-F2].

The evidence is promising, but the provided sources do not establish a strong mechanistic consensus. In the CIPN network meta-analysis, acupuncture was not more effective than massage for pain or peripheral neuropathological symptoms [N1-F1], suggesting that its mechanism may be real but not clearly superior in this specific context.

### 6) Cognitive-behavioral therapy and mindfulness
CBT and mindfulness are highlighted in the chronic pain review as psychological interventions that help patients cope with pain by promoting positive psychological and behavioral changes [N6-F4]. The review also notes that psychological interventions such as CBT and mindfulness-based therapy help patients cope with chronic pain [N2-F2].

Biologically, these approaches may reduce pain through:
- **Expectation and placebo effects**, which can enhance analgesia [N2-F2].
- **Stress reduction and emotion regulation**, which may decrease central sensitization and inflammatory responses [N2-F2].
- **Neuroplastic changes in brain networks** associated with pain processing [N2-F2].

These mechanisms overlap with platinum-induced neuropathy because chronic pain and psychological distress often coexist, and mental health problems can exacerbate pain and disability [N2-F2].

### 7) Spinal cord stimulation
Spinal cord stimulation is discussed in the chronic pain review as a non-invasive non-pharmacological therapy that may be effective for neuropathic pain [N6-F4]. The excerpt notes that patients with neuropathic pain responded better to stimulation than patients with nociceptive pain [N7-R1].

Biologically, SCS may work by:
- **Modulating spinal pain processing** and reducing hyperexcitability [N7-R1].
- **Activating inhibitory pathways** in the spinal cord [N7-R1].

However, the provided evidence does not provide a direct mechanism-specific comparison with platinum-induced neuropathy, so its relevance is indirect.

### 8) Evidence gaps in mechanistic understanding
The biggest mechanistic gap is that, although the evidence is consistent across multiple reviews, the provided sources do not establish a single unified mechanism for each intervention. For example:
- Massage, exercise, heat therapy, and TENS all appear to act at different levels of the pain pathway, but the exact physiological sequence is not fully detailed [N1-F1, N6-F4].
- CBT and mindfulness are supported by psychological and neurophysiological theory, but the provided evidence does not provide a detailed mechanistic model for platinum-induced neuropathy [N2-F2].
- Acupuncture and spinal cord stimulation have plausible mechanisms, but the evidence here does not establish superiority or specificity for platinum-induced neuropathy [N2-F2, N6-F4].

In short, the interventions are biologically plausible and often overlap with the pathophysiology of platinum-induced neuropathy, but mechanistic understanding remains incomplete and heterogeneous [N1-F1, N2-F2, N6-F4].

## Evidence on multimodal approaches and their relative advantages/disadvantages

The provided evidence supports the idea that multimodal non-invasive non-pharmacological therapies (NINPT) are being increasingly explored for chronic pain, including neuropathic pain, and that they may offer broader clinical potential than single interventions.

### 1) Combinations of therapies tested together
The NINPT review explicitly states that these therapies can be used alone or combined with conventional treatments, and that multimodal approaches are being increasingly explored [N6-F4]. It also notes that recent clinical trials demonstrate heat therapy reduces neuropathic pain in chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy [N6-R2]. The review further states that multimodal approaches can be used across chronic pain populations, with physical, psychological, complementary, and alternative approaches included in the package [N6-F4].

From the provided sources, the most directly tested multimodal combinations are:
- **Heat therapy and other NINPT modalities** in chronic pain trials [N6-R2].

Platinum-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is a common and challenging side effect of chemotherapy, often causing pain, sensory dysfunction, motor dysfunction, and impaired quality of life [N1-F1]. ## 1) Which interventions have the strongest evidence?

The strongest evidence comes from a **network meta-analysis** of randomized controlled trials for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). ### Multimodal non-invasive non-pharmacological therapies (NINPT)
The review on NINPT states that these therapies can be used alone or combined with conventional treatments and that they include physical, psychological, complementary, and alternative approaches such as **TENS, heat therapy, cryotherapy, massage, CBT, mindfulness, acupuncture, yoga, and other innovative techniques** [N6-F4]. It also notes that recent clinical trials demonstrate **heat therapy reduces neuropathic pain in chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy** [N6-R2]. While the evidence is not as strong as for massage, multimodal approaches are increasingly recognized as a promising direction for chronic pain management [N6-F4].

### Heat therapy
Heat therapy is explicitly highlighted as part of physical modalities that modulate chronic pain signals through physiological mechanisms [N6-F4]. Recent clinical trial evidence specifically notes that heat therapy reduces neuropathic pain in conditions like diabetic neuropathy and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy [N6-R2]. This makes it a plausible, evidence-informed option for platinum-induced neuropathy.

### Exercise and physical therapy
The physiotherapy review for painful peripheral neuropathies states that physiotherapy and exercise may reduce pain and disability in patients with CIPN and other neuropathies [N3-F3]. It notes that exercise may reduce symptoms in established CIPN, though there is limited evidence for prevention [N3-F3]. The review also emphasizes that interventions targeted at improving motor control or reducing neural mechanosensitivity were common in studies of radicular pain [N3-F3]. This suggests that exercise is a promising approach, especially for improving functional outcomes.

### Cognitive-behavioral therapy and mindfulness
CBT and mindfulness are highlighted as psychological interventions that help patients cope with chronic pain by promoting positive psychological and behavioral changes [N6-F4]. The chronic pain review also notes that psychological interventions such as CBT and mindfulness-based therapy help patients cope with chronic pain [N2-F2]. They may reduce pain through placebo/expectation effects, stress reduction, and emotion regulation [N2-F2]. However, the evidence is more general than specific to platinum-induced neuropathy.

The excerpt notes that patients with neuropathic pain responded better to stimulation than patients with nociceptive pain [N7-R1]. However, the evidence provided is limited and does not establish superiority in platinum-induced neuropathy.

### Bottom line on evidence strength
If ranked by the evidence provided, the strongest-supported interventions are:
1. **Massage** — direct network meta-analysis evidence [N1-F1]
2. **Multimodal NINPT** — promising but less direct evidence [N6-F4]
3. **Heat therapy** — recent clinical trial evidence for neuropathic pain [N6-R2]
4. **Exercise/physical therapy** — promising but less consistent evidence [N3-F3]
5. **CBT/mindfulness** — plausible psychological support, but less strong evidence in the provided sources [N2-F2, N6-F4]
6. **Spinal cord stimulation** — plausible for neuropathic pain, but limited evidence in the provided sources [N6-F4, N7-R1]

---

## 2) Biological and physiological rationale

The evidence points to several mechanisms by which non-pharmacological approaches may reduce pain and improve function in neuropathies. These mechanisms often overlap with the pathophysiology of platinum-induced neuropathy.

### Massage
Massage is described as a physical modality that modulates chronic pain signals through physiological mechanisms [N6-F4]. In the CIPN network meta-analysis, massage was effective for pain and peripheral neuropathological symptoms, suggesting it may reduce pain through mechanical stimulation, gate-control effects, and anti-inflammatory/ neuroprotective actions [N1-F1, N6-F4]. This is especially relevant because platinum-induced neuropathy involves peripheral nerve injury and altered sensory and motor signaling [N1-F1].

Exercise and physical therapy may improve pain and disability by strengthening neural circuits, improving sensorimotor control, and enhancing proprioception and balance [N3-F3]. They may also improve circulation and reduce ischemia-related pain [N6-F4]. These mechanisms overlap with platinum-induced neuropathy, where motor and sensory dysfunction, balance impairment, and reduced quality of life are common [N1-F1].

Heat therapy is described as a physical modality that modulates chronic pain signals through physiological mechanisms [N6-F4]. Recent clinical trials suggest it reduces neuropathic pain in chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy [N6-R2]. Biologically, heat may improve local blood flow, reduce tissue ischemia, and modulate inflammatory and neuroinflammatory processes [N6-F4]. This is especially relevant for platinum-induced neuropathy, which is often associated with microvascular and inflammatory changes in peripheral nerves [N1-F1].

### Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)
TENS is part of the broader NINPT category and is described as a physical modality that modulates chronic pain signals through physiological mechanisms [N6-F4]. It may work through gate-control effects, endogenous opioid release, and modulation of peripheral and central sensitization [N6-F4]. However, the provided evidence does not give a direct effect size for TENS in platinum-induced neuropathy, so its mechanism is plausible but less directly established for this condition [N6-F4].

It is noted as a method used for millennia to relieve pain [N2-R2]. - **Exercise and physical therapy** can be integrated into routine care if physiotherapists or rehabilitation providers are available [N3-F3].

For platinum-induced peripheral neuropathic pain, the best-supported non-pharmacological approaches are **massage**, **multimodal non-invasive non-pharmacological therapies**, **heat therapy**, **exercise/physical therapy**, and **CBT/mindfulness** [N1-F1, N6-F4, N6-R2, N3-F3, N2-F2].
